home.title: Prospekt: lens simulator for iPhone. See what any lens frames on your camera
home.description: Prospekt is an iPhone lens simulator: a live viewfinder that shows what a 14 to 300 mm lens frames on your camera body. 59 bodies, {price} once, works offline.
home.h1: See what any lens frames on your camera, before you buy it
home.lead: Prospekt ({store_name} on the App Store) is an iPhone app that turns your phone into a viewfinder for a lens you don't own yet. Pick your camera body and a focal length from 14 to 300 mm, point the phone, and see the framing live.
home.facts: {price} once. No subscription, no account, no ads. Works offline.
home.hero_caption: What 24, 35, 50 and 85 mm frame on a full-frame camera, drawn over a photo taken at 14 mm.
home.for_1: You're choosing between a 35 mm and a 50 mm, or a 50 and an 85, and want to see the difference before you spend the money.
home.for_2: You have an APS-C or Micro Four Thirds camera and crop factor still confuses you.
home.for_3: You're scouting a location and want to know if your 24-70 is wide enough, or if you need the 70-200.
home.for_4: You're switching systems and want to know what your old lenses become on the new body.
home.for_5: You're learning photography and want to feel what focal lengths look like.
home.how_1: Pick your camera body. 59 are built in, from Canon, Sony, Nikon, Fujifilm, Panasonic, OM System, Leica, Hasselblad, Pentax and Sigma. You can add your own with any crop factor.
home.how_2: Turn the wheel to a focal length from 14 to 300 mm. It clicks at the popular ones. Add a 1.4x or 2x extender if you use one.
home.how_3: Point your iPhone. Prospekt switches between the ultra-wide, wide and telephoto cameras and sets the zoom so the frame matches that lens on that body.
home.how_4: Take a snapshot. It's saved with a watermark showing the focal length, crop factor, full-frame equivalent and aspect ratio (3:2, 4:3, 16:9 or 1:1), so you can compare later.
home.price_includes: Everything: all 59 bodies, your own bodies, extenders, four aspect ratios, snapshots and future updates. No subscription, no in-app purchases, no ads.
home.price_note: Price in the US App Store. Other countries pay the local equivalent.
home.privacy_text: Prospekt collects no data. There is no account, no analytics, no ads and no third-party code. The camera picture stays on your iPhone, and a photo is saved only when you tap the shutter, to your own photo library.
home.limits_1: It shows framing, not background blur. The bokeh of an f/1.4 lens is not simulated.
home.limits_2: Your iPhone's widest camera sets the widest framing you can preview: about 13 mm full-frame equivalent on iPhones with an ultra-wide camera.
home.limits_3: At long focal lengths the iPhone uses digital zoom, so the picture gets soft. The framing is still right.
home.limits_4: Perspective comes from where you stand, not from the lens. Prospekt shows the framing from where you are standing.
home.limits_5: iPhone only, iOS 17 or later. No Android or iPad version.
home.compare_live_calc: No, a sample photo or a diagram
home.compare_cost_cine: From free to paid, built mainly for film crews
home.compare_cost_rent: A rental fee and a deposit
home.compare_note: Calculator sites are free and fine for quick numbers, our own lens comparison tool included. Renting is the only way to see bokeh and how a lens renders. Prospekt sits in between: the real scene, your body, a one-time price.
home.faq_1_q: Is there an app that shows what a lens will look like before I buy it?
home.faq_1_a: Yes. Prospekt shows the framing of any focal length from 14 to 300 mm on your camera body, live through your iPhone camera. It costs {price} once on the App Store.
home.faq_2_q: How can I see the difference between 35 mm, 50 mm and 85 mm?
home.faq_2_a: Pick your body in Prospekt and turn the wheel between the three while you point at the same scene. Without the app, compare them over a sample photo in our free lens comparison tool.
home.faq_3_q: What does a 50 mm lens look like on APS-C?
home.faq_3_a: It frames like a 75 mm lens on full frame, or 80 mm on Canon APS-C, which is a short telephoto. Every body has its own table on the camera pages.
home.faq_4_a: It's how much smaller your sensor is than full frame, measured across the diagonal. Multiply a focal length by it to get the full-frame equivalent: 35 mm on a 1.5x body frames like 52.5 mm.
home.faq_5_a: Yes. It never needs the internet, and there's no account to sign in to.
home.faq_6_q: Does it simulate depth of field or background blur?
home.faq_6_a: No. It shows what the lens frames, which is what decides most lens purchases. Bokeh depends on the aperture, the distance and the lens design, and a phone can't show it honestly.
home.faq_7_a: 59 bodies from 10 brands are built in, across full frame, APS-C, Micro Four Thirds and medium format. For any other camera, add it with its crop factor.
home.faq_8_a: No. You pay {price} once and every update is included.
home.faq_9_a: nakolini, a two-person studio: Vitalii Kikot and Dmytro Hryb. We also make Anonimo and Expenny.
home.faq_10_q: Is Prospekt an alternative to Artemis Director's Viewfinder?
home.faq_10_a: For still photographers, yes. Artemis and Cadrage are director's viewfinders built mainly for filmmakers: cinema cameras, cine lenses and shot planning. Prospekt is built for still photography: pick your stills camera from 59 bodies or add your own, choose a lens from 14 to 300 mm, and see the framing live. If you plan film shoots with cine lenses, a director's viewfinder is the better tool.
tool.title: Lens comparison tool: see what any focal length frames on your camera
tool.description: Free lens comparison tool. Pick your camera and focal lengths or a zoom, see the framing over a photo and how far to stand for a portrait. Full-frame equivalent and angle of view for 59 cameras.
tool.h1: Lens comparison: see what each focal length frames on your camera
tool.lead: Free online lens comparison tool. Pick your camera and the focal lengths or zoom you're deciding between: the frames show what each lens captures from the same spot, and the table shows how much it covers and how far to stand. Use one of our sample photos or your own; your photo never leaves your browser.
tool.focals_label: Focal lengths (tap to add or remove)
tool.photo_focal_label: Your photo's focal length, 35 mm equivalent
tool.photo_focal_hint: Found in the photo's details. The iPhone ultra-wide (0.5x) is about 13 mm, the main camera about 24 to 26 mm.
tool.photo_private: Your photo stays on your device. Nothing is uploaded.
tool.photo_error: This browser can't open that photo. Try a JPEG, PNG or WebP.
tool.photo_focal_missing: The photo doesn't say its focal length, so {focal} is assumed. Change it if you know it.
tool.share_own: Your photo stays on your device, so the link opens with a sample photo.
tool.too_wide: Doesn't fit in this photo: {focal}. The hatched area is what the photo doesn't show.
tool.preview_hint: Tap a frame on the photo, or a row in the table, to see what that lens captures.
tool.soft_note: Long focal lengths are cropped from a wide photo, so they look soft here. The framing is right.
tool.noscript: The interactive tool needs JavaScript. The figure and tables below work without it.
tool.static_caption: On a full-frame camera from the same spot: 24, 35, 50 and 85 mm drawn over a photo taken at 14 mm.
tool.equiv_title: The same framing on different sensors
tool.equiv_intro: To frame like a full-frame lens on a smaller or bigger sensor, divide by the crop factor. The table shows the focal length you need on each format.
tool.math_1: A lens frames like its focal length times the crop factor on full frame. That number is the full-frame equivalent.
tool.math_2: The angle of view is 2 x arctan(sensor size / (2 x focal length)), for the width, the height or the diagonal of the sensor.
tool.math_3: Frames are drawn on a flat (rectilinear) projection, which is how all normal lenses draw. Fisheye lenses are different.
tool.math_4: Micro Four Thirds and 44 x 33 medium format sensors are 4:3, so their frames are taller than the 3:2 frames of full frame and APS-C.
tool.faq_1_q: How do I compare two lenses without buying them?
tool.faq_1_a: Pick your camera above and tap both focal lengths. The frames show what each one captures from the same spot. To see it on a real scene, Prospekt does the same live through your iPhone.
tool.faq_2_q: Is 35 mm or 50 mm better for everyday photos?
tool.faq_2_a: 35 mm shows more of the scene and suits streets, travel and small rooms. 50 mm is tighter and suits portraits and details. Compare both frames on your camera above and pick the one closer to how you see.
tool.faq_3_q: Does the tool work on a phone?
tool.faq_3_a: Yes. It runs in any modern browser, and your own photos are processed on your device.
tool.faq_4_q: How far away do I stand for a full-body portrait?
tool.faq_4_a: On a full-frame camera held vertically, about {d35} with a 35 mm lens, {d50} with 50 mm, {d85} with 85 mm and {d135} with 135 mm. That fits a 1.8 m person in 90% of the frame height. Every camera page lists these distances for that body.
tool.faq_5_q: How far do I stand for a full-body portrait with an 85 mm lens on APS-C?
tool.faq_5_a: About {d85_15} on a 1.5x APS-C camera such as Sony, Fujifilm or Nikon, and {d85_16} on Canon APS-C (1.6x), with the camera held vertically and a 1.8 m person filling 90% of the frame height. Held horizontally, about {d85_15_h} on 1.5x. With a 50 mm lens on 1.5x APS-C, about {d50_15}.
tool.math_5: Coverage at a distance is the distance x sensor size / focal length. It assumes the lens is focused far away. Close up, most lenses frame a little tighter.
tool.zooms_label: Zoom lenses (tap to add both ends)
tool.focal_error: Enter a focal length from {min} to {max}.
tool.zoom_error: Enter two different focal lengths from {min} to {max}.
tool.subject_hint: The subject fills 90% of the frame height. A standing adult is about 1.8 m (6 ft), head and shoulders about 0.5 m (1.6 ft).
tool.distance_note: Covers is the width x height of the scene with the camera held horizontally. Close up, real lenses frame a little tighter than these numbers.
tool.distance_title: What each focal length covers at a distance
tool.distance_intro: On a full-frame camera held horizontally, each lens captures a scene this wide and this tall. On a smaller sensor, use the focal length with the same full-frame look from the table above. 1 m is about 3.3 ft.

tool.portrait_intro: On a full-frame camera held vertically, with the subject filling 90% of the frame height. Full body means a 1.8 m person, head and shoulders about 0.5 m.
tool.portrait_row: {focal}: about {full} for a full-body portrait, {head} for head and shoulders.
tool.portrait_formats_intro: How far to stand so a 1.8 m person fills 90% of the frame height, with the camera held vertically.

guides.description: Short answers to common lens questions, with numbers: 35 mm or 50 mm, 50 or 85, and the best focal length for portraits, street, landscapes, travel, interiors and wildlife on every sensor size.

guides.lead: The lens questions people ask most, answered for full frame, APS-C and Micro Four Thirds. Each page gives the answer first, then the numbers, the trade-offs and a link to compare the frames over a photo.

compare.faq_3_q: What do {a} and {b} frame like on APS-C?
compare.faq_3_a: On a 1.5x APS-C camera, {a} frames like {eq_a} on full frame and {b} like {eq_b}. On Canon APS-C (1.6x), like {eq_a_16} and {eq_b_16}. For the full-frame look on 1.5x APS-C, use about {ff_a} and {ff_b}.
compare.24_35_answer: 24 mm is wider and suits landscapes, interiors and big scenes up close. 35 mm is tighter and more natural, and suits streets, travel and people in their surroundings.
compare.24_35_choose_1: Pick 24 mm for landscapes, architecture and small rooms, where you can't step back far enough for 35 mm.
compare.24_35_choose_2: Pick 35 mm if people are often in the picture. At 24 mm you stand closer, and faces near the edges of the frame look stretched.
compare.24_35_choose_3: With 24 mm you tend to stand close, so near things look big and far things small. That adds depth to a foreground, and makes distant mountains look smaller.
compare.24_35_choose_4: If you have a 24-70 mm zoom, both are on it. Spend a week at each end and see which one you keep coming back to.
compare.28_35_answer: 28 mm is a little wider and suits tight streets, crowds and small rooms. 35 mm is a little tighter and suits people, travel and everyday photos, with less stretching at the edges.
compare.28_35_choose_1: The difference is small. From the same spot, 28 mm shows about 25% more width than 35 mm: {cover_a} against {cover_b} at 3 m.
compare.28_35_choose_2: Pick 28 mm for street photography close to people, in crowds and narrow streets, and for small rooms.
compare.28_35_choose_3: Pick 35 mm if you also take portraits or photograph food and details. It's easier to fill the frame with one subject.
compare.28_35_choose_4: Fixed-lens cameras split the same way: the Ricoh GR and the Leica Q3 are 28 mm, and the Fujifilm X100 series frames like 35 mm.
compare.35_50_answer: 35 mm is wider and suits streets, travel and rooms. 50 mm is tighter and suits portraits and details.
compare.35_50_choose_1: Pick 35 mm if you want one lens for most things: a room, a street, and a person with their surroundings.
compare.35_50_choose_2: Pick 50 mm for portraits and details. For the same framing you stand farther back, so faces look more natural and the background shows less clutter.
compare.35_50_choose_3: At the same aperture and the same framing of a person, 50 mm blurs the background a little more than 35 mm.
compare.35_50_choose_4: A 50 mm f/1.8 is usually the cheapest fast lens in any system. Fast 35 mm lenses tend to cost a bit more.
compare.50_85_answer: 50 mm is the more flexible lens: half-body and full-body portraits, small rooms and everyday photos. 85 mm is the classic portrait lens: head and shoulders, flattering faces and a simple background.
compare.50_85_choose_1: Pick 85 mm if you mostly shoot portraits and have room to step back. A full-body portrait needs about {full_b} between you and the person.
compare.50_85_choose_2: Pick 50 mm if you shoot indoors or want one lens for people and everything else. A full body fits at about {full_a}.
compare.50_85_choose_3: 85 mm keeps you farther from the face, so noses and chins keep their proportions. Its narrower view shows a smaller patch of background, which looks calmer.
compare.50_85_choose_4: Both come as affordable f/1.8 lenses in most systems. The 85 mm ones are bigger and usually cost more.
compare.85_135_answer: 85 mm is the all-round portrait lens and works indoors and out. 135 mm is tighter, needs more room, and gives the simplest background for headshots and outdoor portraits.
compare.85_135_choose_1: Pick 85 mm if you shoot indoors or in mixed places. With 135 mm, a full body needs about {full_b}, which few rooms have.
compare.85_135_choose_2: Pick 135 mm for outdoor portraits, events and stages, where you want a tight frame from far away.
compare.85_135_choose_3: From the same spot, 135 mm makes the subject {ratio} bigger. Step back to keep the same framing, and the background looks bigger and closer, with less of it behind the person.
compare.85_135_choose_4: 135 mm primes are bigger and heavier, and fast ones usually cost more. A 70-200 mm zoom covers both lengths, at the cost of size and weight.

guide.portraits_h1: What is the best focal length for portraits?
guide.portraits_answer: For portraits, 85 mm on full frame is the classic: flattering faces and a simple background. On APS-C, {aps_85} frames about the same, and on Micro Four Thirds, {mft_85}.
guide.portraits_why_1: 85 mm puts you about {head_85} from the person for head and shoulders. From there, noses and chins keep their real proportions, and the narrow view shows only a small patch of background, so it looks calm.
guide.portraits_why_2: 50 mm is the flexible choice: half-body and full-body portraits, small rooms, and people with some of their surroundings. Fill the frame with just a face, though, and you're close enough that noses start to look bigger.
guide.portraits_why_3: 135 mm gives the tightest frame and the simplest background, but a full body needs about {full_135}, so it's mostly an outdoor lens. 35 mm is for environmental portraits, where the place matters as much as the person. Keep faces away from the edges of the frame.
guide.portraits_use_85: The classic: head and shoulders to half body
guide.portraits_use_50: Half body to full body, indoors and out
guide.portraits_use_35: Environmental portraits: a person and their place
guide.portraits_faq_1_a: Yes, for half-body and full-body portraits, and indoors where there's no room to step back. A full body fits at about {full_50} on full frame. For tight headshots, 85 mm flatters faces more, because you stand farther away.
guide.portraits_faq_2_q: What focal length is best for portraits on APS-C?
guide.portraits_faq_2_a: About {aps_85}: on a 1.5x camera it frames like {aps_85_eq}, close to the classic 85 mm. A 50 mm lens on APS-C frames like {eq15_50}, also a good portrait length. On Canon APS-C (1.6x), use about {canon_85}.
guide.portraits_faq_3_q: How far do I stand for a full-body portrait with an 85 mm lens?
guide.portraits_faq_3_a: About {full_85} on full frame and {full_85_15} on 1.5x APS-C, with the camera held vertically and a 1.8 m person filling 90% of the frame height. For head and shoulders, about {head_85} on full frame.
guide.street_name: Best focal length for street photography
guide.street_h1: What is the best focal length for street photography?
guide.street_answer: For street photography, 35 mm on full frame is the most common choice. 28 mm is wider for crowds and narrow streets, and 50 mm keeps more distance. On APS-C, {aps_35} frames like 35 mm, and on Micro Four Thirds, {mft_35}.
guide.street_why_1: 35 mm frames a scene the way you tend to notice it: a person and what's around them. At 3 m it covers about {cover_35}, enough for a shop front or two people talking.
guide.street_why_2: 28 mm covers about {cover_28} at 3 m, so you can stand close in crowds and narrow streets and still fit the scene. At the same aperture and distance, a wider lens also keeps more in focus, which makes zone focusing easier.
guide.street_why_3: 50 mm covers about {cover_50} at 3 m. It picks out faces, gestures and details from farther away, which feels less intrusive, but it leaves out more of the street.
guide.street_use_35: The all-rounder: people in their surroundings
guide.street_use_28: Close up in crowds and narrow streets
guide.street_use_50: Faces and details from farther away
guide.street_faq_1_q: Is 28 mm or 35 mm better for street photography?
guide.street_faq_1_a: 35 mm is the safer start: wide enough for scenes and tight enough for one subject. 28 mm shows about 25% more width from the same spot and suits photographers who like to work close.
guide.street_faq_2_q: What focal length is best for street photography on APS-C?
guide.street_faq_2_a: About {aps_35} for the classic 35 mm look, or {aps_28} for 28 mm. On Canon APS-C (1.6x), about {canon_35}. A 35 mm lens on a 1.5x camera frames like {eq15_35}, which is tighter than most street photographers want.
guide.street_faq_3_q: Is 50 mm too tight for street photography?
guide.street_faq_3_a: Not too tight, but different. At 3 m it covers about {cover_50}, against {cover_35} for 35 mm, so you photograph people and details rather than whole scenes.
guide.landscape_name: Best focal length for landscape photography
guide.landscape_h1: What is the best focal length for landscapes?
guide.landscape_answer: For landscapes, 24 mm on full frame is the most used wide focal length, 16 mm suits dramatic foregrounds, and 70 mm or longer picks out distant hills and layers. On APS-C, {aps_24} frames like 24 mm, and on Micro Four Thirds, {mft_24}.
guide.landscape_why_1: 24 mm fits a wide view, {h_24} across, without pushing the horizon far away. Put something interesting near the camera, and it leads the eye into the picture.
guide.landscape_why_2: 16 mm, {h_16} across, stretches distance: a rock 1 m away looks big and the mountains behind it look small. It's great with a strong foreground and empty without one.
guide.landscape_why_3: A longer lens does the opposite. At 100 m, 70 mm covers a strip about {w100_70} wide and 200 mm about {w100_200}, so you can pick out one hill, one tree or the layers of a far ridge. That's why many landscape photographers carry a 16-35 mm and a 70-200 mm zoom.
guide.landscape_use_35: A calmer view, close to how you see
guide.landscape_faq_1_q: Is 24 mm wide enough for landscapes?
guide.landscape_faq_1_a: For most scenes, yes. It covers {h_24} horizontally on full frame. Go to 16 mm ({h_16}) when you want a big foreground or a whole sky, and you can stand close to it.
guide.landscape_faq_2_q: What focal length is best for landscapes on APS-C?
guide.landscape_faq_2_a: About {aps_24} for the 24 mm look and {aps_16} for 16 mm. On Micro Four Thirds, {mft_24} and {mft_16}. Kit zooms that start at 18 mm on APS-C frame like {eq15_18} at the wide end, which isn't very wide.
guide.landscape_faq_3_q: Do I need a telephoto lens for landscapes?
guide.landscape_faq_3_a: Not to start, but it helps. A wide lens makes distant things small: at 100 m, 24 mm covers a strip about {w100_24} wide and 200 mm about {w100_200}, so a far peak fills much more of the frame.
guide.travel_name: Best focal length for travel photography
guide.travel_h1: What is the best focal length for travel?
guide.travel_answer: For travel, a 24-70 or 24-105 mm zoom on full frame covers most trips. If you carry one prime, 35 mm is the most versatile: {aps_35} on APS-C, {mft_35} on Micro Four Thirds.
guide.travel_why_1: Travel mixes everything: streets, rooms, food, people and the odd landscape. 24 mm fits a square or a church interior, and 70 mm picks out a face or a facade. A standard zoom covers both, so you change lenses less.
guide.travel_why_2: A single 35 mm prime is lighter and usually brighter, so you can shoot indoors and at night without a flash. It's wide enough for streets and tight enough for a person, and you walk for the rest.
guide.travel_why_3: On APS-C the standard zoom is about 16-55 mm, and on Micro Four Thirds 12-40 or 12-60 mm. They frame like 24-80 to 24-120 mm on full frame.
guide.travel_use_35: One lens for streets, rooms and people
guide.travel_faq_1_q: Is a 35 mm prime enough for travel?
guide.travel_faq_1_a: For many people, yes. It covers about {cover_35} at 3 m on full frame, enough for a street scene or a small room, and it's light. You'll miss the very wide and the long shots, like a whole cathedral from inside or a face across a square.
guide.travel_faq_2_q: Is a 24-70 mm or a 24-105 mm zoom better for travel?
guide.travel_faq_2_a: 24-105 mm reaches farther: {h_105} across at the long end, against {h_70} at 70 mm. 24-105 mm f/4 zooms are also usually lighter than 24-70 mm f/2.8 ones, which gather more light.
guide.travel_faq_3_q: What focal length is best for travel on APS-C?
guide.travel_faq_3_a: A standard zoom that starts at 16 mm frames like {eq15_16} at the wide end. One that starts at 18 mm frames like {eq15_18}, noticeably tighter indoors. For a single prime, {aps_35} frames like 35 mm.
guide.interiors_name: Best focal length for interiors and real estate
guide.interiors_h1: What is the best focal length for interiors and real estate?
guide.interiors_answer: For interiors and real estate, 16 to 24 mm on full frame shows a whole room without the stretched look of anything wider. On APS-C, that's about {aps_16} to {aps_24}, and on Micro Four Thirds, {mft_16} to {mft_24}.
guide.interiors_why_1: Rooms are small, so you need a wide view. At 3 m, 16 mm covers about {cover_16} and 24 mm about {cover_24}. From a corner or a doorway, 16 mm fits most of a room.
guide.interiors_why_2: Wider than about 16 mm, furniture near the edges stretches and rooms look bigger than they are, which disappoints people when they visit. Keep the camera level, at about chest height, so walls stay vertical.
guide.interiors_why_3: 24 mm and 35 mm are for corners, kitchens and details: a set table, a fireplace, the view through a door. They look closer to how the room feels in person.
guide.interiors_faq_1_q: Is 16 mm too wide for real estate photos?
guide.interiors_faq_1_a: No, it's the usual choice. It covers {h_16} across on full frame. Below about 14 mm ({h_14}), the edges stretch enough to make a room look bigger than it is.
guide.interiors_faq_2_q: What lens is best for real estate photos on APS-C?
guide.interiors_faq_2_a: A wide zoom that starts at 10 mm, such as a 10-18 or 10-20 mm. On a 1.5x camera, 10 mm frames like {eq15_10} and 16 mm like {eq15_16}. On Canon APS-C (1.6x), 10 mm frames like {eq16_10}.
guide.interiors_faq_3_q: How far back do I stand to fit a 4 m wall?
guide.interiors_faq_3_a: On full frame, with the camera held horizontally, about {wall_16} at 16 mm and {wall_24} at 24 mm. Most rooms give you about that much space from a doorway or a corner, which is why 16 to 24 mm is the usual range.
guide.sports_wildlife_name: Best focal length for sports and wildlife
guide.sports_wildlife_h1: What is the best focal length for sports and wildlife?
guide.sports_wildlife_answer: For sports and wildlife, start at 300 to 400 mm on full frame; small birds need 600 mm. A smaller sensor helps: a 400 mm lens on APS-C frames like {eq15_400}, and a 300 mm lens on Micro Four Thirds like {eq2_300}.
guide.sports_wildlife_why_1: Subjects are far away and often small. At 30 m, 400 mm covers a scene about {w30_400} wide on full frame: one player, or a deer with some room around it.
guide.sports_wildlife_why_2: Most long lenses are zooms: 100-400 mm and 150-600 mm are the common ones, and 70-200 mm suits indoor sports and sidelines close to the action. Fixed 400 and 600 mm lenses are sharper and brighter, and cost and weigh far more.
guide.sports_wildlife_why_3: A smaller sensor gives more reach from the same lens, which is why many wildlife photographers use APS-C or Micro Four Thirds. The focal lengths in the table are mostly the long end of a zoom, not a fixed lens.
guide.sports_wildlife_use_400: Birds and wildlife at a distance
guide.sports_wildlife_use_300: Field sports from the sideline, larger animals
guide.sports_wildlife_faq_1_a: For larger animals, and birds that let you get close, yes. For small birds, most people want 500 to 600 mm on full frame. On APS-C, a 300 mm lens frames like {eq15_300}.
guide.sports_wildlife_faq_2_q: What focal length is best for sports photography?
guide.sports_wildlife_faq_2_a: From the sideline of a field, 300 to 400 mm on full frame. For indoor sports, close action or kids' games, a 70-200 mm zoom. On APS-C, 200 mm frames like {eq15_200}.
guide.sports_wildlife_faq_3_q: Is APS-C better than full frame for wildlife?
guide.sports_wildlife_faq_3_a: For reach, yes: the same lens frames {crop_15} tighter, so 400 mm frames like {eq15_400}. Full frame usually has less noise at high ISO, which helps early in the morning and late in the evening.
